title: Emotions
subtitle: Fear, Anger, Joy, Grief, Love, and Seven Other Everyday Feelings in Twelve Highlights Each

chapters.title: Fear
chapters.subtitle: Freezing in Place, False Alarms, and the Woman Who Poked a Haunted-House Monster
chapters.historical_anchor: In 1986 at Cornell University Medical Center, neuroscientist Joseph LeDoux showed that sound signals from the ear split into two paths: a slow 24-millisecond high road through the thinking cortex and a fast 12-millisecond shortcut straight to the brain's alarm hub, making you flinch at a curved stick before you even know whether it is a snake.
chapters.exit_fact: Although Patient S.M. felt zero fear of snakes, spiders, or haunted houses because calcium deposits had destroyed her amygdala on both sides, inhaling a single breath of 35 percent carbon dioxide triggered an instant panic attack—proving that the suffocation alarm lives deeper in the brainstem.

chapters.title: Anger
chapters.subtitle: Boiling Blood, Costly Payback, and Why Losing Your Temper Protects You From Bullies
chapters.historical_anchor: In 1982 in Berlin, economist Werner Güth ran the first Ultimatum Game experiments: when one player offered a greedy 9-to-1 split of real cash, the second player routinely rejected the offer so both walked away with nothing, proving that people gladly pay money out of their own pocket to punish an unfair deal.
chapters.exit_fact: Unlike fear, which pulls blood away from the skin and leaves the hands icy cold, anger opens blood vessels in the face and hands and raises finger skin temperature by more than a full degree Celsius while preparing the fists to strike.

chapters.title: Joy
chapters.subtitle: Crinkled Eye Corners, Contagious Smiles, and the Difference Between Wanting and Liking
chapters.historical_anchor: In 1862 in Paris, neurologist Guillaume Duchenne used tiny electrical probes on facial muscles to show that a polite fake smile only pulls the corners of the mouth using the cheek muscle, whereas genuine joy also contracts the outer ring of muscle around the eyes—a muscle most people cannot flex on command.
chapters.exit_fact: Psychologists LeeAnne Harker and Dacher Keltner analyzed the 1960 college yearbook photos of 141 women from Mills College and found that students who showed genuine eye-crinkling smiles at age twenty-one scored significantly higher in marital satisfaction and personal well-being thirty years later.

chapters.title: Sadness and Grief
chapters.subtitle: Broken-Heart Adrenaline, Chemical Tears, and Why Bereavement Feels Like Withdrawal
chapters.historical_anchor: In 1969, British psychiatrist Colin Murray Parkes tracked 4,486 widowed men after the death of their wives and discovered that during the first six months of grief, their death rate from heart failure and stroke jumped 40 percent above married men of the same age.
chapters.exit_fact: Humans are the only animals known to shed emotional tears, and biochemist William Frey found in 1981 that tears cried during grief carry 24 percent more protein than tears triggered by raw onion fumes.

chapters.title: Love and Attachment
chapters.subtitle: Prairie Vole Pair Bonds, Mother's Milk Hormones, and Holding a Partner's Hand in Pain
chapters.historical_anchor: In 2006 at the University of Virginia, psychologist James Coan placed married women inside an MRI scanner and warned them of a mild electric shock to the ankle: holding a stranger's hand calmed the brain's threat alarm slightly, but holding a loving husband's hand quieted the alarm almost completely.
chapters.exit_fact: When two romantic partners sit together and look at each other without speaking for three minutes, their heart rates and breathing rhythms synchronize, and when one partner feels pain, their brain waves lock together while the pain drops.

chapters.title: Disgust
chapters.subtitle: Cockroach Juice, Chocolate Fudge, and How a Rotten-Food Reflex Turned Into Moral Outrage
chapters.historical_anchor: In 1986 at the University of Pennsylvania, psychologist Paul Rozin showed that hungry students refused to eat delicious chocolate fudge after watching it molded into the shape of dog feces, and refused to drink apple juice stirred for five seconds with a completely sterile dead cockroach.
chapters.exit_fact: In 2009 at the University of Toronto, psychologist Hanah Chapman wired sensors to people's faces and proved that getting cheated in a money game activates the exact same upper-lip-curling muscle used to spit bitter poison out of the mouth.

chapters.title: Guilt and Shame
chapters.subtitle: The Urge to Hide Versus the Urge to Fix What You Broke
chapters.historical_anchor: Across decades of studies starting in the 1990s, psychologist June Tangney proved that shame and guilt are opposite forces: shame says 'I am a bad person' and drives people to hide or lash out in anger, while guilt says 'I made a bad mistake' and drives people to apologize and repair the damage.
chapters.exit_fact: In Tangney's longitudinal study of 476 county jail inmates released back into the community, prisoners prone to guilt were significantly less likely to be re-arrested within a year, whereas shame-prone prisoners hid their flaws, blamed others, and returned to jail at higher rates.

chapters.title: Envy and Jealousy
chapters.subtitle: Cucumber Tantrums, Silver-Medal Frowns, and the Pain of Watching a Rival Win
chapters.historical_anchor: In 2003 at Emory University, primatologists Sarah Brosnan and Frans de Waal showed that capuchin monkeys happily ate cucumber slices all day until they saw a neighbor monkey receive a sweet grape for the exact same task—at which point the cucumber-paid monkey hurled the vegetable back at the researcher.
chapters.exit_fact: In 1995, psychologists Victoria Medvec, Scott Madey, and Thomas Gilovich filmed Olympic medalists on the podium and proved that bronze medalists smile far more than silver medalists—because bronze winners compare themselves to finishing fourth with nothing, while silver winners torture themselves over losing gold.

chapters.title: Embarrassment
chapters.subtitle: Why Only Humans Blush and How Turning Red Wins Instant Forgiveness
chapters.historical_anchor: In 1872, Charles Darwin called blushing the most peculiar and most human of all expressions because it is the only bodily reaction caused purely by thinking about what other people think of us—and trying to suppress a blush only makes the face burn brighter.
chapters.exit_fact: Unlike every other vein in the human body, the tiny veins inside human cheeks are lined with special adrenaline sensors that widen the blood vessels instead of narrowing them, flooding the face with red blood within five seconds of a social blunder.

chapters.title: Laughter and Play
chapters.subtitle: Ticklish Rats, Play Bows, and Why Group Laughter Bonds Strangers
chapters.historical_anchor: In 1997 at Bowling Green State University, neuroscientist Jaak Panksepp turned on an ultrasonic microphone while tickling laboratory rats and discovered that rats chirp with rapid 50-kilohertz laughter—and chase the researcher's hand begging for more tickles.
chapters.exit_fact: After neuroscientist Robert Provine eavesdropped on 1,200 natural bursts of laughter in shopping malls and city sidewalks, he found that fewer than 20 percent followed anything remotely resembling a joke, and people laugh thirty times more often around others than when they are alone.

chapters.title: Nostalgia
chapters.subtitle: Swiss Mercenary Homesickness, Cold-Room Warmth, and How Old Songs Steady the Mind
chapters.historical_anchor: In 1688 in Basel, Swiss physician Johannes Hofer coined the word 'nostalgia' from the Greek words for homecoming and pain to describe a mysterious wasting fever among young Swiss mercenaries fighting in lowland France who fell ill whenever they heard alpine cowherd songs.
chapters.exit_fact: In 2012, psychologists Xinyue Zhou and Constantine Sedikides discovered that people placed in a chilly 16-degree Celsius room invoke nostalgic memories to warm up, and listening to nostalgic music makes volunteers able to hold their hand in ice-cold water significantly longer.

chapters.title: Gratitude and Awe
chapters.subtitle: Overview Astronauts, Towering Redwood Trees, and How Feeling Small Makes Us Generous
chapters.historical_anchor: In 2015 at the University of California, Berkeley, psychologist Paul Piff and Dacher Keltner stood volunteers inside a grove of 200-foot Tasmanian blue gum eucalyptus trees for sixty seconds and staged an accident where a passerby dropped a handful of pens—and the tree-gazers picked up significantly more pens than volunteers who stared at a tall office building.
chapters.exit_fact: Waiters and waitresses who simply wrote 'Thank you' on the back of a restaurant check saw their tips rise by 11 percent—and when psychologist Martin Seligman asked volunteers to hand-deliver a 300-word gratitude letter to someone they had never properly thanked, their happiness scores stayed elevated for a full month.
